title: Year four close
hookLine: next year: reading the Granth yourself, and living it

lines: A BOOKMARK IS A SMALL PROMISE.
cards: A bookmark sits in a book like a small promise: someone was here, and someone is coming back. All year, this path has been reading around a book.
Lines quoted from it, hymns sung from it, people bowing before it all over the map. But mostly the book has come in pieces, a line at a time, in paraphrase. Today year four closes.
Tomorrow the bookmark moves, and the path puts the Granth itself into your hands.

teach.h: A YEAR CALLED THE WAYS OF THE GURU.
teach.b: First, the year in one breath. It was called the ways of the Guru. It began with the ragas, the musical moods in which the Granth's hymns are arranged.
Then Guru Nanak's longer teachings: the dialogue with the yogis, the poem on the alphabet's letters, the song of the months. Then the Gurus who followed him, and the Ninth Guru's calm.
Then the Tenth Guru's writings, the Khalsa and the shared code, the living streams of the panth and its places, and last, Sikh thought.

teach.h: THE GRANTH AT THE CENTER OF IT ALL.
teach.b: Second, what sat at the center of every block. The ragas are the Granth's own order. The Gurus' teachings are its hymns.

The code is built around it, the streams bow before it, and even the thought came as its lines. All year, the Granth was the hub, and the path stood a little way off, describing it. Third, what changes.
Year five is called the Granth itself, and living it.

teach.h: NEXT: READ A PAGE, THEN WALK IN ORDER.
teach.b: It starts small: how to read a page, the small signs on the letters, what a hymn's heading tells you, where its center line sits.
Then it walks through the Granth in order, from opening pages to closing ones, a reading a day. Not the whole text; a guided walk. Then it turns to living it, through a whole life.
Fourth, one picture from near the Granth's close.
In the Mundavani, Guru Arjan describes the book as a platter. In paraphrase: on this platter lie three things, truth, contentment and reflection, and the nectar of the Name too.
Whoever eats it, whoever savors it, is set free.
Next year, the platter is set down in front of you.

how: Sikhs read the Guru Granth Sahib in the gurdwara, at home from a gutka of daily prayers or a full copy, and also from printed or digital editions with Gurmukhi and translation side by side.

o: the end of year four, and a turn toward the Granth itself
a pause before the path starts over from day one
a final exam on everything taught over the year

s: year five begins by reading the whole Granth at once

games.q: you open the Granth to its first page and it all looks unfamiliar. what does year five do first?
o: skip ahead to the hymns you already know.
learn how to read a page: its signs, its headings, its center line.
wait until you can read it all fluently.
games.why: it starts small: the small signs on the letters, the heading, the center line. then a guided walk, a reading a day.

practice: If you have a gutka, a printed copy or a trusted app, open it to the first page and don't try to read yet: just look at the letters, the lines, the space around them.
If you don't have one near you, picture where you'll read, at what hour, from what copy. If you pray, ask to come to it ready.

wordCard.voice: Year four close. The ways of the Guru, gathered up, and a turn toward the book at the center of them all. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: granth, a book; Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru.

carryVoice: Your line: next, the granth itself. A bookmark, and a promise to come back. See you in year five.
